I'm super excited.

I enjoy these gatherings and events a lot.

Hi everyone, I'm here at B-Size SF 2025 and I'm super excited because I have the chance to speak with an incredible cybersecurity leader, Ayman.
Hi Ayman, how's it going?
Good, how are you?
Good, how are you?
How are you doing?
Good, good.

Anything that stood out to you?

And today, but you know, it's great.
I love the theme and a lot of friends are giving talks.
So I'm looking to catch up on their talks later.
That's awesome.
So for first timers at conferences like B-Sides, are there any tips or tricks to make the most out of it?
You know, it's interesting.
For the first time, there's so much to take in.
Conferences like this, there's so much to take in.
So I think do a little bit of everything is a good approach.
A little bit of talks.
A little bit of the villages.
Talk to some of the vendors.
See what's out there.
Meet some random people.
Talk to random people online, you know, while you're waiting for lunch or whatnot.
I encourage all that kind of stuff.

Or...

Great.

And then, while you're in line,

Start up a conversation.
And that kind of like real world networking, you might make a friend from that.
That's what I'm trying to say.
Great advice.
Thank you.
So another question, as a leader in cybersecurity, what qualities do you look for usually when hiring or building a team?
That's a good question.
I'm looking for someone that can, one, bring skills to the table, so brings existing skills to the table, but also has an ability to adapt, sorry, has an ability to adapt.
So they need to learn a new environment, they need to adapt to what's going on, and not be just siloed in one, like say, their particular position.
I work with a lot of startups, so I'm coming from that lens, and so I'm looking for someone that could, you know,
Not necessarily hitting the ground running is also good, but also someone that can adapt and wear multiple hats and learn quickly.
I think if you could learn quickly and adapt, you'll be great in any field.
Awesome, awesome.
So if someone is starting cybersecurity in 2025, what would you recommend that they would start learning first?
That's a really good question.
I think you could, I mean, you just need to have, so generally, if you're going to start from 2025 now, I don't know where they're coming from.
Are they already employed?
Are they students?
It's a big question.
Do you have like an area maybe?
So if someone is a junior, like either breaking in or one to two years experience in the industry and they want to upskill and everything is changing with AI, so what would be your recommendation?
Yeah, so try to learn, you know, get a broad sense of the security field.
So that's always just good.
Some of the basics.
Always stay on top of news, okay?
Learn how breaches happen because if you're going to, you know, most of the jobs are defenders.
So if you're going to be a defender, you need to learn how a breach happened.
You know, also keep your expectations realistic.
So, you know, a lot of people are really attracted to the pentest part of the field.
But unless you're doing pentesting already, which I encourage anyone to do, go hop on and do some bug bounty and things like that.
But a lot of people are attracted to that and I encourage doing that.
But there's so many areas, so many more areas to the field, as you know, than just pentesting.
There's, you know, even just from like, say, SOC analyst,
Program managers, engineers, architects, building tools, things like that.
Those are all really good skills.
And then from there, I think you mentioned AI.
It's really important to leverage AI to the best of your ability.

How do you think AI will change cybersecurity?
Wow, this is an excellent question.

Listen, the reality is AI is here, like I said before.
And a lot of companies are now adopting AI into their platforms, right?
And then new companies are coming up with AI right from the beginning.
So AI is going to affect everyone, from the analysts all the way to the CISO.

What I would say for those looking to get into the field, listen, AI, there's a lot of stuff in cybersecurity that's not glamorous, that's a lot of grunt work, that's boring, that's annoying, that stuff's going to get replaced right away.
I think sooner than later.
The analyst stuff, the compliance stuff, that's going to at least get augmented.
Everything is going to begin, the first stage is going to be augmented, right?

Not necessarily fully replace teams, but start augmenting or maybe someone, say they have a budget and they have to decide, should they open a headcount for a SOC analyst or should they get a tool to see if it could do 80% of that SOC analyst's job?
What is that person going to do?
At the end of the day, it's a cost decision.
Look at RSA last year or two.
AI is all over the place.
Whether it's actually being used or not, that's debatable.
